commands.desc: Chat slash command: scaffold a new file or project
commands.tooltip: Type /new followed by a description (e.g., '/new Express REST API with auth middleware') to scaffold a new file. Copilot generates the boilerplate structure based on your description and detected project context.

commands.desc: Chat participant: ask about your entire codebase
commands.tooltip: @workspace tells Copilot Chat to index and reason about your entire VS Code workspace, not just the open file. Use it for questions like '@workspace where is the authentication logic?' or '@workspace explain the data flow'.

commands.desc: Chat participant: ask about terminal output or commands
commands.tooltip: @terminal gives Copilot context from your VS Code integrated terminal. Ask '@terminal why did that command fail?' and Copilot reads your terminal output to diagnose the problem.

commands.desc: Chat participant: ask about VS Code settings and features
commands.tooltip: @vscode scopes questions to VS Code itself. Ask '@vscode how do I enable word wrap?' or '@vscode what keybinding opens the terminal?' Copilot answers with VS Code-specific guidance.

commands.desc: Chat variable: reference a specific file in Chat
commands.tooltip: Type #file in Chat to attach a specific file as context. Copilot will prompt you to pick a file from your workspace. Use this to ask 'refactor #file to use async/await' when the file isn't currently open.

commands.desc: Chat variable: reference current editor selection
commands.tooltip: #selection tells Copilot Chat to focus on whatever text you currently have selected in the editor. Equivalent to having selected code when you open Chat, but useful when adding context mid-conversation.

commands.desc: Chat variable: send current open file as context
commands.tooltip: #editor includes the entire content of your currently active editor file as context in the Chat message. Useful for questions like 'are there any security issues in #editor?'

commands.desc: Open interactive Copilot CLI configuration
commands.tooltip: Launches an interactive menu to configure gh copilot behavior — including whether to send optional usage data to GitHub. Settings are stored in your gh config directory (~/.config/gh/).

commands.desc: Toggle Copilot on/off globally in VS Code settings
commands.tooltip: In VS Code, open Settings (Ctrl+,), search 'Copilot', and toggle 'GitHub Copilot: Enable'. You can also click the Copilot icon in the status bar for quick access. Disabling globally is useful when working with sensitive/proprietary code.

commands.desc: Create a .copilotignore file to exclude files from Copilot context
commands.tooltip: A .copilotignore file (same syntax as .gitignore) tells Copilot not to use matching files as context for suggestions. Critical for excluding files with secrets, API keys, or proprietary algorithms from Copilot's training context.

commands.desc: Enable or disable Copilot for specific programming languages
commands.tooltip: In settings.json, add: `"github.copilot.enable": {"*": true, "markdown": false, "plaintext": false}`. The '*' wildcard sets the default; individual languages override it. Useful for disabling in config/secrets files.

commands.desc: Toggle automatic suggestion display (vs manual trigger only)
commands.tooltip: When set to false, Copilot won't show ghost text automatically — you must press Alt+\ to request a suggestion. Useful if you find automatic suggestions distracting or want to retain full control over when Copilot activates.

commands.desc: Force Copilot Chat to respond in a specific language
commands.tooltip: Set to a locale like 'en', 'ja', or 'fr' to force Copilot Chat responses in that language regardless of your VS Code display language. Useful for multilingual teams or language-learning contexts.

commands.desc: Open Copilot inline chat in the VS Code terminal
commands.tooltip: When your cursor is in the VS Code integrated terminal, Ctrl+I opens a Copilot chat overlay for the terminal context. Ask it to suggest commands, explain errors, or fix failed commands — it reads your terminal history as context.

commands.cmd: # Click Copilot sparkle icon in terminal
commands.desc: Use the terminal Copilot button for command suggestions
commands.tooltip: VS Code 1.90+ shows a sparkle (✨) icon in the terminal toolbar. Clicking it opens Copilot Chat pre-populated with your last terminal command and its output — ideal for quickly diagnosing errors without switching context.

commands.desc: Use clear naming to give Copilot better context
commands.tooltip: Copilot's suggestions are heavily influenced by the names in your code. A function named `getUserAuthTokenFromCookie` will generate much better suggestions than one named `getToken`. Naming is the cheapest way to improve Copilot quality.

commands.cmd: # Add a comment describing what the next function does
commands.desc: Use comments as prompts to guide Copilot
commands.tooltip: Write a natural language comment above an empty function body, then press Enter. Copilot treats the comment as a prompt and generates the implementation. E.g., `// Fetch paginated users from the API and cache the result for 5 minutes`.

commands.cmd: # Keep related code in open tabs
commands.desc: Open relevant files to give Copilot more context
commands.tooltip: Copilot uses your open editor tabs as context windows, not just the current file. If you want it to match an existing pattern (e.g., how you format API responses), open a file that shows that pattern before asking for suggestions.

commands.cmd: # Provide example input/output in a comment
commands.desc: Show Copilot an example to generate better implementations
commands.tooltip: Write a comment like `// input: [3,1,2] -> output: [1,2,3]` before a sorting function. Copilot uses examples as specification — especially useful for data transformation functions where the logic isn't obvious from the name alone.

commands.desc: Write the full function signature before the body
commands.tooltip: Defining the function name, parameter types, and return type gives Copilot a precise specification to implement. In TypeScript, a fully-typed signature almost always produces a more accurate body than an untyped one.

commands.cmd: # Use Copilot to generate regex patterns
commands.desc: Describe a regex in plain English and let Copilot write it
commands.tooltip: Write a comment like `// regex to match ISO 8601 date strings` and Copilot will generate the pattern. This is one of Copilot's strongest use cases — regex is notoriously difficult to write from scratch and Copilot handles it well.

commands.cmd: # Ask Copilot Chat to review a PR diff
commands.desc: Paste a diff into Chat and ask for a code review
commands.tooltip: Copy a git diff output and paste it into Copilot Chat with a prompt like 'review this diff for bugs and security issues'. Copilot will analyze the changes and suggest improvements — a lightweight alternative to waiting for a human reviewer.

commands.desc: Paste an error stack trace into Chat and use /fix
commands.tooltip: Copy a full stack trace, paste it into Copilot Chat, and prefix with /fix. Copilot identifies the likely error location, explains the root cause, and proposes a fix. Works well for NullPointerExceptions, TypeErrors, and similar runtime errors.

commands.cmd: # Use Copilot to translate between languages
commands.desc: Ask Chat to convert a function from Python to TypeScript
commands.tooltip: Select a function in one language, open Chat, and type 'convert this to TypeScript'. Copilot handles idiomatic translation — not just syntax conversion — adapting Python's list comprehensions to JS array methods, for example.

commands.cmd: # Ask Copilot to explain a git conflict
commands.desc: Paste a merge conflict into Chat for explanation and resolution
commands.tooltip: Copy the conflicting section (with <<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into Chat and ask 'explain this conflict and suggest how to resolve it'. Copilot examines both sides, explains what changed, and recommends the appropriate merge strategy.

commands.desc: Select slow code and ask Chat to optimize it
commands.tooltip: Select a function you suspect is slow, open Chat, and ask 'optimize this for performance'. Copilot identifies O(n²) loops, unnecessary re-renders, redundant API calls, and other common bottlenecks, suggesting faster alternatives.

commands.cmd: # Use Copilot for SQL query generation
commands.desc: Describe a database query in English and get the SQL
commands.tooltip: Write a comment like `-- Get the top 5 users by total order value in the last 30 days` and Copilot will generate the SQL. Works best when your schema is visible in the same file or an open tab.

commands.desc: Ask Copilot Chat to write a commit message from a diff
commands.tooltip: Run `git diff --staged` in the terminal, copy the output, and paste into Chat with 'write a conventional commit message for this diff'. Copilot follows the conventional commits format (feat/fix/refactor/chore) and summarizes the changes accurately.

commands.desc: Let Copilot generate repetitive patterns automatically
commands.tooltip: Copilot excels at repetitive code — CRUD endpoints, test setup/teardown, serialization methods. Write the first one fully, then start the second with just the function signature. Copilot infers the pattern and fills in the rest.

commands.cmd: # Use Copilot to write shell scripts
commands.desc: Describe what a script should do in a comment block
commands.tooltip: Create a new .sh file, write a multi-line comment describing what the script should do, then let Copilot generate the implementation. Copilot handles argument parsing, error checking (set -euo pipefail), and common patterns like checking if a command exists.

commands.cmd: # Copilot on GitHub.com: press . (period) to open web editor
commands.desc: Open any GitHub repo in a web editor with Copilot Chat
commands.tooltip: On any GitHub repository page, press the period key (.) to open github.dev — VS Code in your browser. Copilot Chat is available there, giving you AI assistance without installing anything locally.

commands.desc: Use Copilot to auto-summarize a pull request on GitHub
commands.tooltip: On a GitHub pull request, click the Copilot icon to generate a plain-English summary of the changes. Copilot reads the diff and writes a structured summary covering what changed, why, and potential areas of concern.

commands.desc: Let Copilot automatically fix CodeQL security findings
commands.tooltip: When GitHub Advanced Security / CodeQL identifies a vulnerability in your code, Copilot Autofix proposes a specific code change to fix it — directly in the GitHub UI. Available on the Security tab of your repository.

commands.desc: Connect internal documentation as Copilot Chat context
commands.tooltip: GitHub Copilot Enterprise lets admins create knowledge bases from internal wikis, runbooks, and documentation. Developers can then ask Copilot Chat questions grounded in company-specific content using the @docs participant.

commands.desc: Set persistent Chat instructions in .github/copilot-instructions.md
commands.tooltip: Create .github/copilot-instructions.md in your repo with instructions like 'Always use TypeScript strict mode' or 'Follow the error handling pattern in src/utils/errors.ts'. Copilot reads this file and applies the instructions to every Chat response in that workspace.

commands.desc: Show help and available flags for copilot suggest
commands.tooltip: Prints usage information, all available flags (-t/--target, --hostname), and examples. Run this when you're unsure about flag syntax or want to see what options are available.

commands.desc: Show help and available flags for copilot explain
commands.tooltip: Prints usage for the explain subcommand including --hostname for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Copilot CLI routes to github.com by default; enterprise users must specify their GHE host.

commands.desc: Open GitHub Copilot CLI feedback form in the browser
commands.tooltip: Opens the GitHub feedback page for the Copilot CLI extension. Use this to report incorrect suggestions, missing features, or bugs — GitHub uses this feedback to improve the model.

commands.desc: Check if GitHub Copilot is experiencing an outage
commands.tooltip: If Copilot suggestions stop appearing or Chat becomes unresponsive, check githubstatus.com. Copilot relies on GitHub's AI infrastructure — outages are uncommon but do happen. Also check your network can reach api.github.com on port 443.

commands.cmd: # VS Code: Developer: Show Logs > GitHub Copilot
commands.desc: View Copilot extension logs in VS Code for debugging
commands.tooltip: Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P), run 'Developer: Show Logs', and select 'GitHub Copilot'. The log shows authentication status, API calls, and any errors. Share this log when filing a support issue.

commands.cmd: # VS Code: GitHub Copilot: Reset Authentication
commands.desc: Clear and refresh Copilot's GitHub auth token in VS Code
commands.tooltip: Open Command Palette and run 'GitHub Copilot: Reset Authentication' if suggestions stop working after a password change or permission update. This clears the cached token and prompts you to re-authenticate.

commands.cmd: # VS Code status bar: Copilot icon
commands.desc: Check Copilot connection status via the status bar icon
commands.tooltip: The Copilot icon in the VS Code status bar (bottom bar) shows connection state. A spinning icon means it's loading; a yellow warning means a problem. Click the icon for quick enable/disable and status details.

commands.desc: Authenticate Copilot in Neovim after installing the plugin
commands.tooltip: After installing github/copilot.vim via your Neovim plugin manager, run :Copilot setup. It displays a one-time code — enter it at github.com/login/device to link your account. Run :Copilot status to confirm it's working.

commands.desc: Toggle Copilot on or off in the current Neovim session
commands.tooltip: These Neovim commands temporarily enable or disable Copilot for the session without changing configuration. :Copilot disable is useful when editing files with sensitive content in your current session.

commands.desc: Accept Copilot inline suggestion in Neovim with Tab
commands.tooltip: Same as VS Code — Tab accepts the current ghost text suggestion. If Tab conflicts with your autocomplete plugin (like nvim-cmp), remap it in your config: `imap <silent><script><expr> <C-J> copilot#Accept()`.

commands.desc: Cycle through Copilot suggestions in Neovim
commands.tooltip: In Neovim with copilot.vim, Alt+] (next) and Alt+[ (previous) cycle through alternative completions, mirroring the VS Code behavior. You can remap these in your init.lua or init.vim to keys that fit your workflow.

commands.desc: Configure Copilot in IntelliJ / PyCharm / WebStorm
commands.tooltip: GitHub Copilot is available as a plugin for all JetBrains IDEs. After installing from the Marketplace, go to Settings > GitHub Copilot to sign in and configure suggestion behavior. Tab accepts, Alt+[ / Alt+] cycle alternatives — same as VS Code.

commands.desc: Edit your zsh configuration file
commands.tooltip: ~/.zshrc is the zsh equivalent of .bashrc — it runs on every new interactive zsh session. If you use Oh My Zsh or Starship, their configuration lines go here. Zsh also reads ~/.zprofile (login shells) and ~/.zshenv (all shells).

commands.desc: Reload zsh config without restarting the terminal
commands.tooltip: Applies your .zshrc changes to the current shell session instantly. If you get errors after sourcing, check for duplicate PATH entries — sourcing appends on each run, so paths can accumulate.

commands.desc: Edit login shell profile (runs once at login)
commands.tooltip: ~/.profile runs only for login shells (SSH sessions, first terminal on a desktop). Put PATH modifications and environment variables here rather than .bashrc if you want them set once, not on every subshell. Bash reads this before .bashrc on login shells.

commands.desc: Edit bash-specific login profile
commands.tooltip: If this file exists, bash reads it instead of ~/.profile on login. A common pattern is to have .bash_profile source .profile (for shared settings) and then .bashrc (for interactive features). Many users just use .bashrc for everything.

commands.desc: Change your default shell to zsh
commands.tooltip: chsh (change shell) updates your login shell in /etc/passwd. You must log out and back in for the change to take effect. The shell must be listed in /etc/shells. Install zsh first with `sudo apt install zsh`.

commands.desc: List all available shells on the system
commands.tooltip: Shows every shell that chsh will accept as a valid login shell. If zsh or fish isn't listed after installation, you may need to add it manually with `sudo echo /usr/bin/zsh >> /etc/shells`.

commands.desc: Show the shell you are currently running
commands.tooltip: Unlike $SHELL (which shows your login shell), $0 shows the actual shell process running right now. Useful when you've typed `zsh` inside a bash session — $SHELL still says bash but $0 says zsh.

commands.desc: Display your current bash prompt format string
commands.tooltip: PS1 (Prompt String 1) defines what your command prompt looks like. Special sequences like \u (username), \h (hostname), \w (working directory), and \$ (# for root, $ for others) are expanded. Color codes use \[\033[...m\] escapes.

commands.desc: Set a colored bash prompt (green user@host, blue path)
commands.tooltip: This is Ubuntu's default colored prompt. \033[01;32m is bold green, \033[01;34m is bold blue, \033[00m resets to default. The \[ and \] brackets tell bash these are non-printing characters so it calculates line width correctly.

commands.desc: Minimal modern prompt — blue path with orange arrow
commands.tooltip: Uses 256-color escape codes (38;5;N where N is 0–255). This creates a clean, minimal prompt similar to popular modern shells. The ❯ character is a Unicode arrow used by many prompt frameworks. Add this line to ~/.bashrc to make it permanent.

commands.desc: Add the current git branch to your bash prompt
commands.tooltip: Runs `git branch` on every prompt render, extracts the active branch name, and displays it before the working directory. This is a basic approach — for a faster, richer git prompt, consider Starship or __git_ps1 from git's bash completion.

commands.desc: Set the terminal tab title to the current directory name
commands.tooltip: PROMPT_COMMAND is a bash variable that runs a command before each prompt. The escape sequence \033]0;...\007 sets the terminal window/tab title. ${PWD##*/} strips the path to just the folder name. Useful when you have many tabs open.

commands.desc: Install Starship cross-shell prompt
commands.tooltip: Starship is a blazing-fast, highly customizable prompt written in Rust. It works with bash, zsh, fish, and others — one config for all shells. After installing, add `eval "$(starship init bash)"` or `eval "$(starship init zsh)"` to your shell config.

commands.desc: Activate Starship prompt in bash
commands.tooltip: Add this line to the end of ~/.bashrc. Starship replaces your PS1 with a feature-rich prompt showing git status, language versions (Node, Python, Rust), command duration, and more — all with zero configuration out of the box.

commands.desc: Activate Starship prompt in zsh
commands.tooltip: Add this line to the end of ~/.zshrc. If you use Oh My Zsh, put it after the `source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh` line so Starship overrides the Oh My Zsh theme.

commands.desc: Apply the 'Pure' minimal Starship preset
commands.tooltip: Starship ships with several presets (pure, nerd-font-symbols, pastel-powerline, etc.). This command exports a preset to your config file. Edit ~/.config/starship.toml to further customize modules, colors, and symbols.

commands.desc: Edit Starship configuration file
commands.tooltip: Starship uses a single TOML file for configuration. Each module (git_branch, nodejs, python, etc.) has its own section. You can disable modules, change symbols, set colors, and control formatting. See starship.rs/config for all options.

commands.desc: Apply the Nerd Font symbols Starship preset
commands.tooltip: This preset uses special icons from Nerd Fonts (a patched font with thousands of icons). You must install a Nerd Font first (e.g., FiraCode Nerd Font) and set it as your terminal emulator's font — otherwise you'll see empty boxes instead of icons.

commands.desc: Install Oh My Zsh (zsh framework with themes and plugins)
commands.tooltip: Oh My Zsh is the most popular zsh configuration framework. It comes with 150+ themes, 300+ plugins, and a community-driven plugin ecosystem. It modifies your ~/.zshrc to source its framework. Requires zsh to be installed first.

commands.desc: Change your Oh My Zsh theme
commands.tooltip: The ZSH_THEME variable in ~/.zshrc controls your prompt theme. 'robbyrussell' is the default. Popular alternatives: 'agnoster' (powerline-style, needs Nerd Font), 'af-magic', 'bira'. Set to "random" to try a new one each session.

commands.desc: Enable Oh My Zsh plugins in .zshrc
commands.tooltip: The plugins=() array in ~/.zshrc activates Oh My Zsh plugins. 'git' adds 100+ git aliases (gst, gco, gp). Third-party plugins like zsh-autosuggestions and zsh-syntax-highlighting must be cloned into ~/.oh-my-zsh/custom/plugins/ first.

commands.desc: Update Oh My Zsh to the latest version
commands.tooltip: The omz command is Oh My Zsh's built-in CLI. `omz update` pulls the latest changes from the GitHub repository. Oh My Zsh also checks for updates automatically every 2 weeks by default.

commands.desc: List all available Oh My Zsh themes
commands.tooltip: Oh My Zsh ships with 150+ themes in this directory. Each .zsh-theme file defines a prompt style. Preview them all at github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/wiki/Themes to find one you like without trying each one manually.

commands.desc: Create a detailed directory listing alias
commands.tooltip: Aliases create shorthand commands in your current session. -l (long format), -A (show hidden files except . and ..), -h (human sizes), --color=auto (colored output). Add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc to make it permanent.

commands.desc: Create a short alias for git status
commands.tooltip: Single-letter or two-letter aliases for frequently used commands save enormous time. Common git aliases: gs (status), ga (add), gc (commit), gp (push), gd (diff). Define them in your shell config file.

commands.desc: Navigate up one directory with double-dot
commands.tooltip: Navigation aliases are among the most-used shortcuts. Extend the pattern: ...='cd ../..' or ....='cd ../../..' for going multiple levels up. Some shells (zsh) support this natively with the AUTO_CD option.

commands.desc: Always colorize grep output
commands.tooltip: Makes grep highlight matches in red by default. Ubuntu often sets this in /etc/bash.bashrc, but adding it explicitly ensures it works everywhere. Also set for egrep and fgrep.

commands.desc: Make rm ask for confirmation before deleting
commands.tooltip: -i (interactive) prompts before each deletion. A safety net against accidental `rm important_file`. If you need to override it temporarily, use `\rm` (backslash escapes the alias) or `command rm`.

commands.desc: Check if a command is an alias, function, or binary
commands.tooltip: The `type` builtin tells you what a command name resolves to: alias, shell function, builtin, or external binary path. Essential for debugging when a command behaves unexpectedly — it might be aliased to something you didn't expect.

commands.desc: Create a directory and cd into it in one step
commands.tooltip: Shell functions are more powerful than aliases — they accept arguments ($1, $2, etc.) and can contain logic. This classic function creates a directory (with -p for nested paths) and immediately changes into it. Add to .bashrc/.zshrc.

commands.cmd: extract() { case "$1" in *.tar.gz) tar xzf "$1" ;; *.zip) unzip "$1" ;; *.gz) gunzip "$1" ;; *) echo "Unknown" ;; esac; }
commands.desc: Universal extract function — handles tar.gz, zip, gz, etc.
commands.tooltip: Instead of remembering different flags for each archive type, this function detects the extension and runs the right command. Extend the case statement for .bz2, .xz, .7z, .rar as needed.

commands.desc: Function to check what's using a specific port
commands.tooltip: Type `port 3000` to see which process is listening on port 3000. Saves you from typing the full lsof command each time. Useful during development when port conflicts are frequent.

commands.desc: Create a timestamped backup of a file
commands.tooltip: Type `backup important.conf` and it creates `important.conf.bak.20260414190000`. The date format creates a sortable timestamp. Safer than overwriting a single .bak file each time.

commands.desc: Install zsh syntax highlighting plugin
commands.tooltip: Highlights commands as you type: valid commands in green, errors in red, strings in yellow. Makes typos instantly visible before you press Enter. After installing, add `source /usr/share/zsh-syntax-highlighting/zsh-syntax-highlighting.zsh` to .zshrc.

commands.desc: Activate syntax highlighting in your current zsh session
commands.tooltip: This line must go at the end of ~/.zshrc (after all other plugins). If you use Oh My Zsh, clone the plugin to ~/.oh-my-zsh/custom/plugins/ instead and add it to the plugins=() array.

commands.desc: Install zsh-autosuggestions for Oh My Zsh
commands.tooltip: zsh-autosuggestions shows faint grey completions based on your command history as you type. Press the right arrow key to accept the full suggestion, or Ctrl+Right to accept one word at a time. One of the most impactful terminal productivity plugins.

commands.desc: Install zsh-syntax-highlighting for Oh My Zsh
commands.tooltip: Clones the plugin into Oh My Zsh's custom plugin directory. After cloning, add 'zsh-syntax-highlighting' to the plugins=() array in ~/.zshrc. Must be the last plugin in the array to work correctly.

commands.desc: Customize autosuggestion text color
commands.tooltip: Controls the color of the ghost text suggestion. 240 is a medium grey (256-color). Set to a lighter value (245–250) if your terminal background makes 240 hard to see. Add to .zshrc before the plugin is sourced.

commands.desc: Set autosuggestion sources to history first, then completion
commands.tooltip: By default, autosuggestions only use command history. Adding 'completion' as a fallback means you also get tab-completion-style suggestions when no history match exists. Makes the plugin useful even for commands you've never typed.

commands.desc: Install fzf — the command-line fuzzy finder
commands.tooltip: fzf is a general-purpose fuzzy search tool that transforms the terminal experience. It powers Ctrl+R (history search), Ctrl+T (file search), and Alt+C (cd into directory). After installing, source the keybinding scripts in your shell config.

commands.desc: Enable fzf keybindings and completion in bash
commands.tooltip: Add to ~/.bashrc. Binds Ctrl+R (search command history interactively), Ctrl+T (insert a file path from fuzzy search), and Alt+C (cd into a directory found by fuzzy search). Transforms how you navigate files and history.

commands.desc: Enable fzf keybindings and completion in zsh
commands.tooltip: Add to ~/.zshrc. Same keybindings as bash (Ctrl+R, Ctrl+T, Alt+C). If using Oh My Zsh, you can alternatively add 'fzf' to the plugins array which handles sourcing automatically.

commands.desc: Customize fzf appearance (inline, reversed, bordered)
commands.tooltip: --height 40% shows fzf inline instead of fullscreen. --layout=reverse puts the search input at the top (more natural). --border draws a box around results. Add to .bashrc/.zshrc. Many users also add --preview for file previews.

commands.desc: Use fd instead of find for fzf file search (much faster)
commands.tooltip: By default, fzf uses `find` which is slow on large directories. fd (install with `sudo apt install fd-find`) is 5–10x faster, respects .gitignore, and excludes hidden files by default. --hidden includes dotfiles, --exclude .git skips the git directory.

commands.desc: Show syntax-highlighted file previews in fzf
commands.tooltip: When you press Ctrl+T, fzf shows a preview panel with syntax-highlighted file contents using bat (install with `sudo apt install bat`). This turns fzf into a visual file browser. Press Enter to insert the selected file path.

commands.desc: Preview directory contents when fuzzy-finding with Alt+C
commands.tooltip: Shows the contents of each directory as you scroll through Alt+C results. Lets you see what's inside a folder before cd-ing into it. Combine with eza (modern ls replacement) for even better previews.

commands.desc: Enable vim keybindings in your shell
commands.tooltip: Switches bash/zsh to vi editing mode. Press Escape to enter normal mode (navigate with h/j/k/l, delete with d, etc.), press i to return to insert mode. Dramatically faster for editing long commands if you know vim. Add to .bashrc/.zshrc.

commands.desc: Enable emacs keybindings in your shell (default)
commands.tooltip: Emacs mode is the default for most shells. Ctrl+A (beginning of line), Ctrl+E (end), Ctrl+W (delete word back), Ctrl+K (kill to end). If you've switched to vi mode and want to go back, use this.

commands.desc: Enable vim mode in zsh
commands.tooltip: The zsh equivalent of `set -o vi`. Enables vi-style keybindings. Pair with KEYTIMEOUT=1 in .zshrc to reduce the delay when pressing Escape (default is 0.4 seconds, which feels sluggish).

commands.desc: Reduce zsh vi-mode Escape key delay to 10ms
commands.tooltip: KEYTIMEOUT is measured in hundredths of a second. The default (40 = 400ms) makes Escape feel laggy. Setting to 1 (10ms) makes mode switching feel instant. Essential for a usable vi-mode experience.

commands.desc: Edit readline configuration (bash key bindings)
commands.tooltip: ~/.inputrc configures GNU readline, which controls input for bash and many CLI programs (python REPL, mysql, etc.). You can remap keys, enable case-insensitive tab completion, and set editing preferences that apply globally.

commands.desc: Make tab completion case-insensitive
commands.tooltip: By default, bash tab completion is case-sensitive (typing 'doc' won't complete 'Documents'). Adding this to ~/.inputrc makes it case-insensitive — a small change that saves constant frustration.

commands.desc: Show all completions on first Tab press (no double-tap)
commands.tooltip: Normally bash requires you to press Tab twice when there are multiple completions. This setting shows all options on the first press. Faster and more predictable — you always see what's available immediately.

commands.desc: Color-code tab completion results by file type
commands.tooltip: Makes tab completion results use the same colors as `ls --color` — directories in blue, executables in green, symlinks in cyan. Helps you visually distinguish file types without pressing Enter.

commands.desc: List all active readline keybindings in bash
commands.tooltip: Shows every key combination and what it's bound to. Useful for finding available key slots when you want to add custom bindings, or for discovering useful shortcuts you didn't know existed.

commands.desc: Up arrow searches history matching current input (zsh)
commands.tooltip: By default, Up arrow just goes to the previous command. This binding makes it search history for commands starting with what you've already typed. Type 'git' then press Up — only git commands appear. One of the most productive zsh bindings.

commands.desc: Down arrow searches history forward matching current input (zsh)
commands.tooltip: Pairs with the Up arrow binding above. After searching backward through matching history entries, Down arrow goes forward again. Together they create a type-and-filter history experience similar to fzf.

commands.desc: Keep 50,000 commands in memory history
commands.tooltip: HISTSIZE controls how many commands are kept in memory during the current session. The default (500–1000) is too small for power users. Setting to 50,000+ means you can search months of history. Add to .bashrc/.zshrc.

commands.desc: Save up to 100,000 commands in the history file
commands.tooltip: HISTFILESIZE controls how many lines are written to ~/.bash_history when a session ends. Set it equal to or larger than HISTSIZE. For zsh, use SAVEHIST instead of HISTFILESIZE.

commands.desc: Save up to 100,000 commands in zsh history file
commands.tooltip: The zsh equivalent of HISTFILESIZE. Zsh writes to ~/.zsh_history. Combined with `setopt SHARE_HISTORY`, all open terminals share the same history file in real time.

commands.desc: Ignore duplicates and commands starting with space in history
commands.tooltip: ignoreboth = ignorespace + ignoredups. Commands prefixed with a space aren't saved (useful for commands with passwords). erasedups removes older duplicates when a command is repeated. Keeps history clean and searchable.

commands.desc: Share command history between all open zsh sessions
commands.tooltip: By default, each zsh session has its own history. SHARE_HISTORY writes and reads the history file in real time across all terminals. A command typed in one tab is immediately available via Ctrl+R in another.

commands.desc: Append to bash history file instead of overwriting
commands.tooltip: By default, bash overwrites ~/.bash_history when a session exits. If you have multiple terminals, only the last one to close wins. histappend makes all sessions append, preserving history from every terminal.

commands.desc: Install Alacritty GPU-accelerated terminal emulator
commands.tooltip: Alacritty renders using your GPU via OpenGL, making it one of the fastest terminals available. It's configured entirely through a TOML file — no GUI settings. Minimal, no tabs/splits built in (use tmux for that). Written in Rust.

commands.desc: Create and edit the Alacritty config file
commands.tooltip: Alacritty reads from ~/.config/alacritty/alacritty.toml. Changes are applied instantly on save — no restart needed. The file controls fonts, colors, opacity, padding, scrollback, keybindings, and shell settings.

commands.desc: Set font family and size in Alacritty
commands.tooltip: Font configuration in the [font] section. Use a Nerd Font for icon support in Starship and other tools. Install fonts with `sudo apt install fonts-firacode` or download Nerd Font versions from nerdfonts.com.

commands.desc: Set Alacritty window transparency and blur
commands.tooltip: opacity ranges from 0.0 (fully transparent) to 1.0 (opaque). blur applies a Gaussian blur to the content behind the window. Requires a compositor (most modern Ubuntu desktops have one). Set to ~0.90–0.95 for a subtle see-through effect.

commands.desc: Install Kitty GPU-accelerated terminal emulator
commands.tooltip: Kitty is a fast, feature-rich terminal with built-in tabs, splits, image rendering, and ligature support. GPU-accelerated via OpenGL. Configured through ~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf. Has a built-in kitten framework for extensions.

commands.desc: Edit Kitty configuration file
commands.tooltip: kitty.conf uses simple key=value syntax. Hundreds of options: fonts, colors, transparency, keybindings, tab layout, cursor style, and more. Run `kitty +kitten themes` for an interactive theme selector.

commands.desc: Browse and apply Kitty color themes interactively
commands.tooltip: Opens a built-in theme browser with live preview. Scroll through themes with arrow keys and press Enter to apply. Includes hundreds of themes (Dracula, Nord, Catppuccin, etc.). Selected theme is written to kitty.conf automatically.

commands.desc: Set the font in Kitty
commands.tooltip: Kitty supports font ligatures out of the box — coding ligatures like -> => != render as single glyphs if your font supports them. Set bold_font, italic_font, and bold_italic_font separately for precise control.

commands.desc: Set window transparency in Kitty
commands.tooltip: Values from 0.0 (fully transparent) to 1.0 (opaque). Unlike Alacritty, Kitty also supports per-tab transparency and can dim inactive tabs. Requires a compositor. Set dynamic_background_opacity yes to toggle at runtime.

commands.desc: SSH with Kitty's terminal features forwarded to remote
commands.tooltip: Kitty's SSH kitten forwards Kitty's terminfo to the remote server so features like undercurl, colored underlines, and image rendering work over SSH. Avoids the common problem of missing terminfo entries on remote machines.

commands.desc: Install WezTerm GPU-accelerated terminal with Lua config
commands.tooltip: WezTerm is a GPU-accelerated terminal configured with Lua scripts. It has built-in multiplexing (tabs, splits, workspaces), image support, and ligatures. Its Lua config is extremely flexible — you can script dynamic behavior that other terminals can't do.

commands.desc: Edit WezTerm configuration file
commands.tooltip: WezTerm uses a Lua script for configuration — more powerful than TOML/ini files because you can use variables, conditionals, and functions. The file returns a config table. Changes apply on save.

commands.desc: Set the font in WezTerm via Lua config
commands.tooltip: WezTerm has excellent font rendering with ligature support. Use wezterm.font('Name', {weight='Bold'}) for specific weights. You can also set config.font_size and config.line_height.

commands.desc: Set a color scheme in WezTerm
commands.tooltip: WezTerm ships with 700+ built-in color schemes. Set config.color_scheme to any scheme name. Run `wezterm ls-fonts --list-system` to see available fonts and schemes. Popular: 'Catppuccin Mocha', 'Tokyo Night', 'Dracula'.

commands.desc: Set window transparency in WezTerm
commands.tooltip: Like other GPU-accelerated terminals, WezTerm supports background transparency. Pair with config.macos_window_background_blur (macOS) or a compositor on Linux for blur effects behind the window.

commands.desc: Install FiraCode font with programming ligatures
commands.tooltip: FiraCode is a monospaced font designed for code. Ligatures combine character sequences like ->, =>, !=, and === into single glyphs. After installing, set it as your terminal emulator's font. For Nerd Font icons, download FiraCode Nerd Font from nerdfonts.com.

commands.cmd: # Install a Nerd Font for icons in Starship, powerlevel10k, etc.
commands.desc: Download and install a Nerd Font (nerdfonts.com)
commands.tooltip: Nerd Fonts are patched versions of popular fonts with 3,000+ icons added (git symbols, language logos, file type icons). Required for many prompt themes. Download the Nerd Font version of your preferred font, extract, and install with `fc-cache -fv`.

commands.desc: Rebuild the system font cache after installing fonts
commands.tooltip: After placing .ttf or .otf files in ~/.local/share/fonts/ (user) or /usr/share/fonts/ (system), run this to update the font cache. -f forces a rebuild even if timestamps haven't changed, -v shows verbose output so you can verify your font was found.

commands.desc: Check if a specific font is installed
commands.tooltip: fc-list shows all fonts the system knows about. Pipe to grep to search for a specific name. If your font doesn't appear after installing, run fc-cache -fv to rebuild the cache. The output shows the file path, family name, and style.

commands.desc: Install bat — syntax-highlighted cat replacement
commands.tooltip: bat is like cat but with syntax highlighting, line numbers, git diff integration, and automatic paging. On Ubuntu the binary is called `batcat` (to avoid conflict with another package). Create an alias: `alias bat='batcat'`.

commands.desc: Install exa — modern ls replacement with git integration
commands.tooltip: exa (or its maintained fork 'eza') shows colored output, file icons (with Nerd Fonts), git status per file, and tree views. Common aliases: `alias ls='exa --icons'`, `alias ll='exa -lah --icons --git'`, `alias tree='exa --tree'`.

commands.desc: Install fd — fast, user-friendly find replacement
commands.tooltip: fd is 5–10x faster than find, has simpler syntax (`fd pattern` instead of `find . -name 'pattern'`), respects .gitignore by default, and uses smart case matching. On Ubuntu the binary is called `fdfind` — alias it: `alias fd='fdfind'`.

commands.desc: Install ripgrep (rg) — fast grep replacement
commands.tooltip: ripgrep searches file contents 2–5x faster than grep by searching in parallel and skipping binary/gitignored files automatically. Syntax: `rg pattern` (recursive by default). Supports regex, file type filters, and context lines.

commands.desc: Install zoxide — smarter cd that learns your habits
commands.tooltip: zoxide tracks which directories you visit and ranks them by frequency. After installing, `eval "$(zoxide init bash)"` replaces cd with z. Type `z proj` and it jumps to /home/user/workspace/my-project if that's where you go most often.

commands.desc: Activate zoxide in bash (replaces cd with z)
commands.tooltip: Add to ~/.bashrc. After a few days of use, zoxide builds a database of your directory visits. Then `z` followed by any partial path fragment takes you to the best match. `zi` opens an interactive fzf-powered selector.

commands.desc: Activate zoxide in zsh
commands.tooltip: Add to ~/.zshrc. Works the same as in bash. Zoxide stores its database in ~/.local/share/zoxide/db.zo. The algorithm considers both frequency (how often) and recency (how recently) you visited a directory.

commands.desc: Install tldr — simplified man pages with examples
commands.tooltip: tldr shows practical examples for a command instead of the full manual. Type `tldr tar` to see the 5 most common tar recipes. Community-maintained and available for almost every common command. Much faster than reading man pages.

commands.cmd: # MCP: Model Context Protocol — the standard for AI tool use
commands.desc: MCP connects AI agents to external tools and data sources
commands.tooltip: Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 and now supported by Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI, is an open standard for connecting AI agents to tools. Think of it as a 'USB for AI' — one protocol that lets any compatible agent talk to any MCP server (databases, GitHub, file systems, web search, etc.).

commands.desc: Install the official MCP CLI tools globally
commands.tooltip: The MCP CLI provides utilities for testing MCP servers, inspecting available tools, and running servers locally. Required for developing and debugging MCP server implementations before connecting them to an agent.

commands.desc: Launch the MCP Inspector to debug MCP servers visually
commands.tooltip: The MCP Inspector is a browser-based GUI for connecting to an MCP server and exploring its tools, resources, and prompts. Run it locally, point it at your server URL, and test tool calls interactively before wiring up an agent.

commands.desc: View Claude Desktop's MCP server configuration
commands.tooltip: Claude Desktop stores its MCP server connections in this JSON file. Each server entry specifies a command to launch the server process (usually npx or python) and any environment variables it needs. Edit this file to add new MCP servers.

commands.desc: Start the MCP filesystem server for a directory
commands.tooltip: Runs the official MCP filesystem server, exposing read/write file operations as MCP tools. Any connected agent can then list files, read contents, and write changes. The path argument limits access to that directory tree.

commands.desc: Start the MCP GitHub server (requires GITHUB_TOKEN env var)
commands.tooltip: Exposes GitHub operations as MCP tools: list repos, create issues, open PRs, read file contents. Set GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token before running. Connected agents can interact with GitHub repositories without browser access.

commands.desc: Start the MCP PostgreSQL server for database access
commands.tooltip: Exposes your PostgreSQL database as MCP tools. Agents can run SELECT queries, inspect schemas, and describe tables. Set the DATABASE_URL environment variable to your connection string. Read-only by default for safety.

commands.desc: Start the MCP Brave Search server for web search
commands.tooltip: Gives connected agents real-time web search capability via the Brave Search API. Set BRAVE_API_KEY in your environment. Agents can call brave_web_search as a tool to fetch current information beyond their training cutoff.

commands.desc: Start the MCP memory server for persistent agent knowledge
commands.tooltip: The MCP memory server stores key-value facts that persist between agent sessions. Agents can store observations, preferences, and learned context, then retrieve them in future sessions. Useful for personalization and long-running workflows.

commands.desc: Start the MCP Puppeteer server for browser automation
commands.tooltip: Exposes browser automation as MCP tools: navigate URLs, click elements, fill forms, take screenshots, and extract page content. Agents can autonomously browse the web and interact with sites. Requires Chrome or Chromium installed.

commands.desc: Install a Python MCP server with uv (fast Python runner)
commands.tooltip: uvx runs Python packages without installing them permanently — similar to npx for Node. Many MCP servers are published as Python packages. Use `pip install mcp` for the Python SDK, or `uvx` for one-off server execution.

commands.desc: Install the Python MCP SDK for building custom MCP servers
commands.tooltip: The official MCP Python SDK lets you build custom MCP servers in Python. A server exposes tools (functions the agent can call), resources (files/data the agent can read), and prompts (reusable templates). See modelcontextprotocol.io for the full spec.

commands.desc: Run an MCP server over stdio (standard input/output transport)
commands.tooltip: MCP supports two transports: stdio (process launched by the client, communicates via stdin/stdout) and HTTP/SSE (server runs independently). Stdio is simpler for local tools. HTTP is needed for remote or shared servers.

commands.desc: Install Claude Code — Anthropic's agentic CLI coding tool
commands.tooltip: Claude Code is an AI coding agent that lives in your terminal. It reads your codebase, writes and edits files, runs commands, and iterates on tasks autonomously. It uses MCP natively and reads CLAUDE.md for project context. Requires an Anthropic API key or Claude subscription.

commands.desc: Start an interactive Claude Code session in the current directory
commands.tooltip: Launches Claude Code in the current directory. Claude indexes your codebase, reads CLAUDE.md if present, and opens an interactive REPL. You can ask it to implement features, fix bugs, refactor code, or run shell commands on your behalf.

commands.cmd: claude -p 'Add input validation to the login form'
commands.desc: Run Claude Code with a one-shot prompt (non-interactive)
commands.tooltip: -p (--print) runs a single prompt and exits. Useful for scripting or running Claude Code in CI pipelines. Claude reads the codebase, makes changes, and outputs a summary. Combine with --output-format json for programmatic use.

commands.desc: Limit which tools Claude Code can use in a session
commands.tooltip: By default, Claude Code has access to Bash, file Read/Write, and other tools. Restricting with --allowedTools limits what it can do — useful in automated pipelines where you want code changes but not arbitrary command execution.

commands.desc: Start Claude Code with a custom MCP server configuration
commands.tooltip: Points Claude Code at a JSON file defining MCP servers to connect. Each server adds tools Claude can use: database queries, GitHub operations, web search. This is how you give Claude Code access to your specific infrastructure.

commands.desc: View the Claude Code project context file
commands.tooltip: CLAUDE.md is a markdown file at the root of your project that Claude Code reads before every session. It should contain: architecture overview, key conventions, file structure, what to avoid, and any gotchas. Treat it as an onboarding document for the AI agent.

commands.desc: Create a CLAUDE.md project context file for Claude Code
commands.tooltip: Create this file in your project root and fill it with conventions, constraints, and context that Claude Code should always know. Keep it under 500 words — only what the agent can't figure out by reading the code. This dramatically improves suggestion quality.

commands.desc: Show token usage and estimated cost for the current session
commands.tooltip: Displays a breakdown of input/output tokens consumed and the estimated API cost for the current session. Helps you track spending, especially during long autonomous tasks where many tool calls are made.

commands.desc: Clear the conversation context in Claude Code
commands.tooltip: Resets the conversation history and context window. Use when you've finished one task and want to start fresh — carrying over irrelevant context can confuse the agent and waste tokens.

commands.desc: Show Claude Code's current auth and model status
commands.tooltip: Displays current authentication method, active model, MCP server connections, and permission settings. Run this to confirm your API key is working and the right model is selected before starting a long task.

commands.desc: Use the Gemini custom tools endpoint for better tool calling
commands.tooltip: gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools is a separate endpoint (released Feb 19, 2026) optimized for workflows that mix bash execution with custom tool calls. It prioritizes your defined tools over the model's built-in behaviors — recommended for agent pipelines.

commands.desc: Start Gemini CLI with a GitHub MCP server connected
commands.tooltip: Gemini CLI added native MCP support in early 2026. The --mcp-server flag launches a server process and connects it to the session. Gemini can then call GitHub tools (list issues, read files, create PRs) as part of its responses.

commands.desc: Switch Gemini CLI model interactively mid-session
commands.tooltip: The /model slash command opens an interactive model selector inside Gemini CLI. Choose Auto (smart routing), Pro (always 3.1 Pro), or Manual (pick specific model ID). Auto routing uses 3-flash-preview for simple tasks and 3.1-pro-preview for complex ones.

commands.cmd: gemini -p 'Analyze this codebase and suggest improvements' --yolo
commands.desc: Run Gemini CLI autonomously without confirmation prompts
commands.tooltip: --yolo (auto-approve all actions) lets Gemini execute bash commands, write files, and make tool calls without asking for confirmation each time. Use for trusted automated tasks only — the agent operates with full autonomy.

commands.desc: Install OpenAI Codex CLI — GPT-powered coding agent
commands.tooltip: Codex CLI is OpenAI's terminal-based coding agent. It reads your codebase, executes commands, and makes changes autonomously. It reads AGENTS.md for project context (analogous to Claude's CLAUDE.md). Requires an OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable.

commands.desc: Start an interactive Codex CLI session
commands.tooltip: Launches the Codex CLI REPL in the current directory. Type tasks in plain English. The agent can read files, run tests, and make code changes. By default it asks for confirmation before executing shell commands.

commands.desc: Run Codex CLI in full-auto mode (no confirmations)
commands.tooltip: -a full-auto grants the agent permission to execute all actions without prompting. It will run test commands, read error output, edit code, and repeat until tests pass. Use in sandboxed environments — full-auto gives the agent significant autonomy.

commands.desc: Run Codex CLI with a specific OpenAI model
commands.tooltip: Specify which OpenAI model powers the agent with -m. Options include o4-mini (fast, cheap), o3 (more capable), and gpt-4.1 (balanced). o4-mini is the default as of 2026 — it's fast enough for most coding tasks at lower cost.

commands.desc: Create an AGENTS.md project context file for Codex CLI
commands.tooltip: AGENTS.md is Codex CLI's equivalent of CLAUDE.md — project conventions, architecture, and constraints for the agent. Multiple AI tools recognize this file: Codex CLI, some Copilot variants, and others. If you use multiple agents, AGENTS.md is the most widely supported.

commands.desc: Install Goose — open-source AI agent by Block
commands.tooltip: Goose is an open-source, extensible AI coding agent by Block (formerly Square). It supports multiple LLM backends (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Ollama) and has a rich plugin system called 'toolkits'. MCP-compatible and runs entirely locally if paired with Ollama.

commands.desc: Start a new Goose agent session
commands.tooltip: Opens an interactive Goose session. Goose automatically discovers MCP servers configured in its profile, loads toolkits, and starts a conversation. It can execute shell commands, edit files, and call external APIs based on your instructions.

commands.desc: Resume the most recent Goose session with full context
commands.tooltip: Goose saves session history locally so you can continue where you left off. The agent reloads its previous context window and tool state. Useful for long multi-session projects — you don't lose the thread of what the agent was working on.

commands.cmd: goose run --with-toolkit developer 'Set up a FastAPI project'
commands.desc: Run Goose with the developer toolkit for coding tasks
commands.tooltip: --with-toolkit loads additional capability bundles. The 'developer' toolkit adds code analysis, testing, and shell tools. Other toolkits: 'github', 'jira', 'google-drive'. You can combine multiple with repeated flags.

commands.desc: Configure Goose — set LLM provider, API keys, toolkits
commands.tooltip: Opens an interactive configuration wizard. Set your AI provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama), API key, default model, and default toolkits. Config is stored in ~/.config/goose/profiles.yaml.

commands.desc: Install aider — AI pair programmer for Git repos
commands.tooltip: aider is a command-line AI coding tool that integrates tightly with Git. It edits files, creates commits automatically (with descriptive commit messages), and tracks changes in your repo. Works with Claude, GPT, Gemini, and local Ollama models.

commands.desc: Start aider in the current Git repo (uses default model)
commands.tooltip: Launches aider in the current directory. It reads your repo structure and opens an interactive chat. Files you mention are added to the context. aider writes all changes and automatically commits them — making your AI editing history trackable in git log.

commands.desc: Run aider with Gemini 3.1 Pro as the coding model
commands.tooltip: aider supports dozens of models via litellm. Use the provider/model-id format. For Gemini, set GEMINI_API_KEY. aider benchmarks different models monthly — check aider.chat/docs/leaderboards for current rankings.

commands.desc: Run aider with Claude as the coding model
commands.tooltip: Claude models consistently rank highly on aider's coding benchmarks. Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Claude's large context window is useful for aider since it loads entire files into context for editing.

commands.desc: Run aider with a local Ollama model (free, private)
commands.tooltip: aider can use locally-running Ollama models for completely free and private AI coding. Qwen2.5-Coder is one of the strongest open-weight coding models. Run `ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b` first. Slower than cloud models but no API costs.

commands.desc: Enable automatic Git commits after each AI edit
commands.tooltip: aider will commit every change it makes with a descriptive message like 'aider: Implement user auth middleware'. Creates a clean history of AI-assisted changes that you can review, revert, or cherry-pick. Enabled by default in most configs.

commands.desc: Disable automatic Git commits (review changes before committing)
commands.tooltip: Use when you want to review and optionally squash/amend changes before committing. aider still stages changes — run `git diff --staged` to review and `git commit` manually when satisfied.

commands.desc: Load context files into aider without making them editable
commands.tooltip: --read adds files to the context as read-only references. The agent uses them for guidance but won't modify them. Perfect for architecture docs, style guides, and convention files that should inform edits without being edited themselves.

commands.desc: Enable aider's lint and test loop for autonomous fixing
commands.tooltip: aider will run your test suite after each edit and automatically attempt to fix failures — creating a tight feedback loop. --lint enables linting checks too. The agent iterates until tests pass or it gives up. Very powerful for TDD workflows.

commands.desc: Start the Ollama model server (local AI inference)
commands.tooltip: Ollama runs AI models locally on your CPU/GPU. `ollama serve` starts the HTTP server on localhost:11434. Once running, any MCP-compatible agent or tool can use it as a local, free, private model backend.

commands.desc: Download Llama 3.3 70B model for local use
commands.tooltip: Downloads the model weights from Ollama's registry. 70B means 70 billion parameters — very capable but requires ~40GB RAM or a GPU with that VRAM. For most machines, smaller models like llama3.3:8b or qwen2.5-coder:7b are more practical.

commands.desc: Download Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B — strong coding model for low-end hardware
commands.tooltip: Qwen2.5-Coder is purpose-built for coding tasks and punches above its weight at 7B parameters. Runs on most modern laptops with 8GB RAM. Use with aider or any Ollama-compatible agent for free local coding assistance.

commands.desc: List all locally installed Ollama models
commands.tooltip: Shows every model you've downloaded with its size and when it was last modified. Use this to see what's available before starting an agent session, and to identify old models you can remove with `ollama rm`.

commands.cmd: ollama run llama3.3 'Explain how async/await works in Python'
commands.desc: Run a one-shot prompt with a local Ollama model
commands.tooltip: Runs a single prompt and prints the response to stdout. Useful for quick queries and for scripting AI responses into shell pipelines. Add --format json to get structured output for programmatic use.

commands.desc: Call the Ollama API directly from the command line
commands.tooltip: Ollama exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API on port 11434. Calling it directly lets you integrate local AI into any script. The stream:false flag returns the complete response at once instead of streaming tokens. Use jq to extract fields.

commands.desc: Start Ollama server exposed on all network interfaces
commands.tooltip: By default Ollama only listens on localhost. Setting OLLAMA_HOST to 0.0.0.0 makes it accessible from other machines on your network — useful for running Ollama on a powerful desktop and connecting from a laptop. Secure with a firewall rule.

commands.desc: View the AGENTS.md universal agent context file
commands.tooltip: AGENTS.md is recognized by Codex CLI, some Copilot variants, and other agents as project-level context. If you use multiple AI tools, maintain AGENTS.md as the canonical source and have CLAUDE.md reference it. Keep it concise — under 500 words.

commands.desc: Create Claude Code project-level settings
commands.tooltip: Claude Code reads .claude/settings.json for project-specific configuration: allowed tools, MCP server definitions, and model preferences. These settings override your global ~/.claude/settings.json for this project only.

commands.desc: Add an MCP server to Claude Code's project config
commands.tooltip: In .claude/settings.json, add to the 'mcpServers' object: {"name": {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"], "env": {"GITHUB_TOKEN": "..."}}}. Claude Code connects to this server automatically when you open the project.

commands.desc: Install the Anthropic Python SDK for Claude API access
commands.tooltip: The official SDK for calling Claude models programmatically. Supports streaming, tool use (function calling), and multi-turn conversations. Claude's tool use feature is the foundation for building agents — the model decides when to call tools and processes results.

commands.desc: Install the Google Generative AI Python SDK for Gemini
commands.tooltip: The official Python SDK for Gemini API access. Supports all Gemini models including 3.1-pro-preview, function calling, MCP integration, and streaming. Use gemini-3.1-pro-preview-customtools model ID for agents with heavy tool use.

commands.desc: Install the OpenAI Python SDK
commands.tooltip: The OpenAI SDK provides access to GPT, o-series, and other OpenAI models. It also powers any library using the OpenAI-compatible API standard — including Ollama, Together, Groq, and many others that mirror OpenAI's API interface.

commands.desc: Install LangChain — agent and chain orchestration framework
commands.tooltip: LangChain provides building blocks for LLM applications: chains (sequences of operations), agents (LLMs that decide which tools to call), memory, and retrieval. langchain-community adds integrations with hundreds of tools and data sources.

commands.desc: Install LangGraph — stateful multi-agent workflow framework
commands.tooltip: LangGraph builds on LangChain to create stateful, cyclical agent graphs. Agents can loop, branch, and pass state between nodes — enabling multi-step workflows that simple chains can't handle. The recommended way to build complex agent pipelines in 2026.

commands.desc: Install LiteLLM — unified interface for 100+ LLM providers
commands.tooltip: LiteLLM normalizes the API interface across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Cohere, Ollama, and 100+ others. Write your code once against the OpenAI interface; switch models by changing a string. Essential for building provider-agnostic agents.

commands.desc: Start a LiteLLM proxy server for local model access
commands.tooltip: Runs a local OpenAI-compatible API proxy that routes to Ollama or any configured backend. Any tool that speaks the OpenAI API (including many agent frameworks) can now use your local model without code changes. Useful for testing locally before switching to cloud.

commands.desc: Set your Anthropic API key for Claude access
commands.tooltip: Set this in your shell session or in ~/.bashrc for persistence. Never hardcode API keys in source code — use environment variables or a secrets manager. Claude Code, aider, LangChain, and most agent frameworks read this variable automatically.

commands.desc: Set your OpenAI API key
commands.tooltip: Required for Codex CLI, aider with GPT/o-series models, LiteLLM, and direct OpenAI SDK use. Store in a .env file for project-specific keys and load with `source .env` or `dotenv` — never commit .env to Git.

commands.cmd: pip install python-dotenv && dotenv run -- python agent.py
commands.desc: Load .env file and run an agent script with those variables
commands.tooltip: python-dotenv reads a .env file and injects its KEY=VALUE pairs as environment variables. `dotenv run --` passes them to the following command without permanently exporting them. Best practice: create a .env file, add it to .gitignore, and load it this way.

commands.cmd: claude -p 'Plan the implementation' | gemini -p 'Implement the plan'
commands.desc: Pipe Claude's plan output into Gemini for implementation
commands.tooltip: CLI agents can be composed with Unix pipes. Claude generates a plan, its output becomes Gemini's input. This multi-agent pattern lets you use each model's strengths: Claude for reasoning/planning, Gemini for code generation, for example.

commands.cmd: gemini -p "$(cat requirements.txt)" 'Generate a Docker setup for these dependencies'
commands.desc: Pass file contents into an agent prompt via command substitution
commands.tooltip: $(cat file) substitutes the file's contents into the prompt string. This is how you feed local context (requirements, logs, configs) into CLI-based agents. For large files, use --context-file flags where available instead.

commands.desc: Run an AI log monitor every 60 seconds
commands.tooltip: watch re-runs a command at an interval. Combined with a CLI agent, you create a simple AI-powered monitoring loop. The agent checks recent log lines and prints analysis. For production use, pipe the output to a notification system.

commands.cmd: git diff HEAD~1 | claude -p 'Review this diff for bugs and security issues'
commands.desc: Pipe a git diff into Claude for automated code review
commands.tooltip: Passes the diff of the last commit to Claude for review. Add to a pre-push Git hook to get AI review before every push. The agent reads the diff from stdin and outputs findings. Useful as a first-pass review before human review.

commands.cmd: find . -name '*.py' | xargs cat | gemini -p 'Find all TODO comments and suggest implementations'
commands.desc: Scan an entire codebase for TODOs and get AI suggestions
commands.tooltip: Chains find, cat, and a CLI agent to process all Python files at once. Note: for large codebases this may exceed context limits. Use `--model gemini-3.1-pro-preview` for the largest context window (up to 1M tokens).

commands.desc: Run an AI coding agent inside a Docker sandbox
commands.tooltip: Isolating agents in Docker containers limits blast radius if the agent makes unintended changes — it can only affect the mounted volume, not your host system. Essential for running agents in --yolo/full-auto mode safely.

commands.cmd: # Use --allowedTools to whitelist specific agent capabilities
commands.desc: Restrict agent tool access to a safe subset
commands.tooltip: Most CLI agents support tool allowlisting. Limiting tools prevents the agent from taking unexpected actions — for example, allowing Read but not Write during exploration, or allowing Bash but not network access. Defense-in-depth for autonomous agents.

commands.cmd: # Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in a project .env, add .env to .gitignore
commands.desc: Best practice: never commit API keys to Git
commands.tooltip: API keys in Git history are a serious security risk — even deleted keys can be found in history. Use a .env file, add it to .gitignore, and load with dotenv. For CI/CD, use GitHub Secrets or your platform's secret management.

commands.desc: Check token usage and cost breakdown for the Claude session
commands.tooltip: Shows cumulative token usage and estimated API spend for the current Claude Code session. Agentic sessions can consume tokens quickly — especially when the agent reads many files. Set a budget alert in your Anthropic account dashboard.

commands.desc: Limit max tokens per Claude API response
commands.tooltip: Setting a max token limit prevents runaway responses from consuming large amounts of your quota. For agent tasks, 4096 is usually sufficient for each step. The agent makes multiple calls, each capped at this limit.

commands.desc: View LiteLLM proxy logs to debug agent tool calls
commands.tooltip: When your agent uses LiteLLM as a proxy, this command shows every API call made: model, prompt length, response time, and cost. Invaluable for debugging unexpected behavior and understanding what the agent is actually sending to the model.

commands.desc: Install Rich — beautiful terminal output for agent scripts
commands.tooltip: Rich is a Python library for colorful, formatted terminal output: tables, progress bars, syntax-highlighted code, markdown rendering. Essential for agent scripts that need to display structured results clearly in the terminal.

commands.desc: Install Typer — build CLI interfaces for agent scripts
commands.tooltip: Typer creates CLI tools from Python functions using type hints. Add a --model flag, --verbose option, and auto-generated --help documentation to your agent scripts with minimal code. Used by many agent frameworks internally.

commands.desc: Install httpx — async HTTP client for agent API calls
commands.tooltip: httpx is the modern async-first HTTP client for Python. Essential for building agents that call multiple APIs concurrently — you can make 10 tool calls simultaneously instead of sequentially, dramatically speeding up multi-step workflows.

commands.desc: Install Pydantic — data validation for structured agent outputs
commands.tooltip: Pydantic validates and parses structured data using Python type hints. Use it to define output schemas for your agents — the model outputs JSON, Pydantic validates it matches your schema and raises clear errors if it doesn't. Essential for reliable agent pipelines.

commands.desc: Install Instructor — structured AI outputs using Pydantic models

commands.tooltip: Compiles the Android app and installs it on a connected device or running emulator, then launches it. Requires the Android SDK and a device reachable via adb. Debug builds connect to the Metro server.

commands.desc: Build and launch the app in the iOS simulator
commands.tooltip: Compiles the iOS app and boots it in the default simulator. Requires Xcode and CocoaPods dependencies installed (pod install). Pass --simulator "iPhone 16" to pick a specific device.

commands.desc: Stream Android device logs in real time
commands.tooltip: Tails logcat output for the running app, filtered to React Native messages. Use it to watch console.log output and native crashes while developing. Press Ctrl+C to stop.

commands.desc: Stream iOS simulator logs in real time
commands.tooltip: Tails the iOS system log for the app running in the simulator. Useful for seeing JS console output and native errors side by side with the Metro terminal.

commands.desc: Check the React Native environment for issues
commands.tooltip: Runs health checks on your setup: Node version, JDK, Android SDK, CocoaPods, and Xcode. Reports what is missing or outdated — the first thing to run when builds fail mysteriously.

commands.desc: Show the resolved project configuration
commands.tooltip: Prints the effective React Native configuration: project paths, asset roots, platforms, and dependency versions. Useful for debugging why a native module is or is not linked.

commands.desc: List connected Android devices and emulators
commands.tooltip: adb (Android Debug Bridge) is the universal tool for talking to Android devices. This prints every connected device/emulator with its serial. A device showing 'unauthorized' needs a USB debugging permission prompt accepted.

commands.desc: Open an interactive shell on a connected device
commands.tooltip: Drops you into a Linux shell running on the Android device itself. From there you can inspect files, run commands, or check system state — the same environment your app runs in.

commands.desc: Install an APK, keeping app data
commands.tooltip: Installs an Android package file (.apk). The -r flag reinstalls and preserves the app's existing data, which is useful when iterating on builds without wiping local state. Use adb install -r -d to allow a downgrade.

commands.desc: Uninstall an app by package name
commands.tooltip: Removes an app from the device using its package identifier (the 'applicationId' in your build.gradle). Find the package name with adb shell pm list packages.

commands.desc: Forward a device port to the host machine
commands.tooltip: Makes the device's port 8081 connect to your computer's port 8081 over USB — this is how a physical Android phone reaches the Metro dev server without Wi-Fi. Run it after plugging in a new device.

commands.desc: Show only React Native JavaScript logs
commands.tooltip: logcat is Android's system log. The -s flag filters to the ReactNativeJS tag, so you see console.log output from your JS code without the noise of every other system message.

commands.desc: Dump Android crash stack traces
commands.tooltip: -d dumps the log buffer and exits (instead of streaming forever). Filtering to AndroidRuntime with severity E shows fatal crashes — the Java stack traces from native crashes in your app.

commands.desc: List user-installed apps on the device
commands.tooltip: pm (package manager) lists installed packages. The -3 flag limits output to third-party apps, excluding the system's own packages. Useful for finding the exact package name of an app you installed.

commands.desc: Force-stop an app
commands.tooltip: am (activity manager) force-stops an app's process entirely — like swiping it away plus killing background work. Use this to get a clean app start during testing, which is more reliable than just pressing back.

commands.desc: Show the current activity stack
commands.tooltip: dumpsys prints internal system service state. This variant shows which activity is in the foreground — handy for verifying deep-link routing or confirming which screen your app actually opened.

commands.desc: Copy a file from the device to your computer
commands.tooltip: Copies a file (or directory) from the device's filesystem to your current local directory. Useful for grabbing logs, screenshots, or databases your app wrote to storage.

commands.desc: Copy a file from your computer to the device
commands.tooltip: Copies a local file onto the device. Common uses: pushing an APK to test, seeding test data, or dropping files into app-visible storage paths.

commands.desc: Reboot the connected device
commands.tooltip: Restarts the Android device. Pair with adb wait-for-device afterwards if your script needs to continue once the device is back online.

commands.desc: Wait until a device is connected
commands.tooltip: Blocks until adb sees a device. Combine with adb reboot in shell scripts to pause until the phone finishes restarting before running the next adb command.

commands.desc: Build the debug APK
commands.tooltip: gradlew is the Gradle wrapper — a project-local script that uses the exact Gradle version the project pins. assembleDebug compiles the debug variant and outputs app-debug.apk under android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/.

commands.desc: Build and install the debug APK
commands.tooltip: Shortcut that builds the debug variant and immediately installs it on a connected device. Faster than assembling and adb install separately when you are iterating.

commands.desc: Build the release AAB for Play Store upload
commands.tooltip: Produces the Android App Bundle (.aab), the format Google Play requires for uploads. Play then generates optimized APKs per device from the bundle. Requires release signing configured.

commands.desc: Run Android lint checks
commands.tooltip: Android Lint statically analyzes your code for bugs, accessibility issues, and performance problems. Run it in CI to catch issues before they reach users. Reports land in android/app/build/reports/.

commands.desc: Run the Android unit tests
commands.tooltip: Executes the unit tests in the test/ source set (JVM tests that do not need a device). Add --tests "com.example.FooTest" to run a single class.

commands.desc: List all available Gradle tasks
commands.tooltip: Prints every task the project can run, grouped by type. Run this to discover what build, test, and install tasks exist in your Android project without guessing names.

commands.desc: List installed and available Android SDK packages
commands.tooltip: sdkmanager (in cmdline-tools/latest/bin) manages Android SDK components: platforms, build-tools, and platform-tools. --list shows what is installed versus available, including the license acceptance status.

commands.desc: List available Android virtual devices
commands.tooltip: Lists every AVD (Android Virtual Device) you have created — named configurations of device profile, system image, and storage. The names here are what you pass to emulator -avd.

commands.desc: Boot a specific Android emulator
commands.tooltip: Starts the emulator with the named AVD. Add -no-snapshot-load for a cold boot, or -no-window to run headless (CI-friendly). The emulator binary lives in $ANDROID_HOME/emulator/.

commands.desc: Show an APK's package name, version, and permissions
commands.tooltip: aapt2 (Android Asset Packaging Tool) reads an APK's manifest metadata. dump badging prints the package name, versionCode/versionName, launchable activity, and permissions — the fastest way to verify what a build actually contains.

commands.desc: Run a Maestro UI test flow
commands.tooltip: Maestro is a UI-testing framework for mobile apps driven by simple YAML flows. This runs the named flow against the app currently on the device or emulator. Flows describe taps, text input, and assertions in plain steps.

commands.desc: Open Maestro Studio to record and inspect UI
commands.tooltip: Launches an interactive studio on top of the connected device: it shows the live view hierarchy and lets you point-and-click to generate test steps. Great for building flows without memorizing selectors.

commands.desc: Print the current UI hierarchy for selectors
commands.tooltip: Dumps the accessibility tree of the screen currently shown. Use the text, id, or accessibility labels you see here to write robust Maestro selectors instead of guessing at element identifiers.

commands.desc: Install CocoaPods dependencies for iOS
commands.tooltip: CocoaPods is the dependency manager for iOS native libraries. pod install resolves the Podfile and generates the .xcworkspace file — always open and build the workspace, not the .xcodeproj, after running it.

commands.desc: Run pod install without a global CocoaPods install
commands.tooltip: The pod-install package bundles CocoaPods, so you do not need a system-wide gem install. Recommended by React Native docs when CocoaPods is missing on a fresh machine.

commands.desc: List schemes and targets in an Xcode project
commands.tooltip: xcodebuild is the command-line interface to Xcode builds. -list prints the project's schemes and targets — the exact names you need for -workspace and -scheme flags in later commands.

commands.desc: Build the iOS app from the command line
commands.tooltip: Compiles the app using the workspace and scheme, in Release configuration. This is what CI runs to produce the .app bundle. Add -sdk iphonesimulator to build for the simulator instead of a device.

commands.desc: List available iOS simulators
commands.tooltip: simctl is the CLI for controlling the iOS Simulator. list devices shows every simulator (including 'Shutdown' ones) with their UDIDs — the identifier you use to boot or target a specific simulator.

commands.desc: Boot an iOS simulator
commands.tooltip: Starts the named simulator headlessly — no Simulator window needed. Pair with open -a Simulator if you want the UI, or xcrun simctl bootstatus to wait until boot completes.

commands.cmd: npx react-native bundle --platform android --dev false --entry-file index.js --bundle-output android-release.bundle
commands.desc: Bundle JavaScript for release without Metro
commands.tooltip: Pre-compiles all JS into a single bundle file, so the release build does not need the dev server. Run this before a standalone APK when you want the JS baked in. --dev false enables production optimizations.

commands.desc: Set up Fastlane for a project
commands.tooltip: Fastlane automates iOS/Android release chores (signing, screenshots, uploads). init creates the Fastfile, Appfile, and folder structure, and asks for your app's identifiers.

commands.desc: Run a named Fastlane lane
commands.tooltip: A lane is a named sequence of actions defined in the Fastfile. This executes the 'release' lane — whatever build, signing, and upload steps you defined there. List lanes with fastlane lanes.

commands.desc: Authenticate wrangler with your Cloudflare account
commands.tooltip: Opens your browser for OAuth and stores the token locally so wrangler can act as you. Run this once per machine before deploying or managing resources.
